casualties.looks: Lying very still beside a bent scooter. Breathing slowly, and noisily.
casualties.stays: Nothing. He snores.
casualties.why: Slow, noisy breathing and no answer to a command: his brain is in trouble. Red.

casualties.who: Young woman with a bleeding leg
casualties.looks: A dupatta tied tight round her thigh. She tied it herself. She's very calm.
casualties.stays: She can't stand on that leg. She doesn't try twice.
casualties.why: Over two seconds for the nail bed to pink up: the bleeding has beaten her knot. Red.

casualties.looks: Shouting into his phone about a meeting. A small cut over one eye.
casualties.walks: He walks to the kerb, still on the phone, still late.

brief.easy: Six off the first ambulances from the festival grounds. Red now, yellow soon, green walks, black beyond help. The rules are on the card. In order.
brief.hard: Eight of them, and the grounds are still emptying. The loud ones aren't the sick ones. You know that. Prove it.
brief.extreme: Ten, and I'm needed inside. No card, no checks from me. The rules are in your head, Chief.

tagged.yellow: Yellow. {who} can wait, but not long.
tagged.green: Green. To the gate, please, and wait for a nurse.

sent.all: Every tag right. Sending them in.
sent.some: Sending them in. Dr. Iyer will check the tags again inside.
sent.under: Sending them in. Chief, one you tagged to wait is going grey.

casualties.short: the boy with the burnt hand
casualties.looks: His hand in a bucket of water somebody gave him. A rocket went off in his fist.
casualties.walks: He walks to the gate with his bucket. Sore, scared, and going to be fine.

casualties.who: Woman in a green sari, coughing
casualties.looks: Sitting by the firework stall, breathing fast and shallow. She says it's only the smoke.
casualties.stays: She tries to stand and can't find her breath.
casualties.why: Over thirty breaths a minute is red, however she explains it. Hot smoke swells the airways shut.

casualties.who: Man pulled from under the stage
casualties.short: the man from under the stage
casualties.looks: Dragged out from under the fallen stage. Not moving.
casualties.stays: No answer at all.
casualties.why: He wasn't breathing until you opened his airway, then he was. That's red, and every second counts.

casualties.short: the girl with the painted face
casualties.looks: Face painted like a tiger, a grazed knee, asking where her mother is.
casualties.walks: She walks to the gate holding a volunteer's hand. Stripes still on.

casualties.short: the woman by the sweet stall
casualties.looks: Lying by the sweet stall, pale and clammy. She says it's only the crowd.
casualties.stays: She can't get up. She says she'll rest a minute.
casualties.why: A nail bed slow to pink up means blood loss you can't see. That's red.

casualties.looks: Fell off the gate, climbing for a better view. His wrist has an extra bend in it.
casualties.stays: He gets halfway up and sits back down, green in the face.

casualties.looks: Under the main beam of the stage. Eyes open, not moving.
casualties.stays: No answer.

casualties.who: Boy in a new kurta, silent
casualties.looks: Sitting by the gate, staring at nothing. Not a mark on him.
casualties.stays: He doesn't move when you ask. He doesn't look at you.
casualties.why: He couldn't follow a simple command: a head injury until proven otherwise. Red.

casualties.looks: Lying on his side by the gate, holding his chest. Short, quick breaths.
casualties.stays: He tries, gasps, and lies back.
casualties.why: Over thirty breaths a minute is red: ribs broken in the crush, and a lung struggling under them.

casualties.who: Woman pulled out of the crowd
casualties.looks: The crowd parted round her a minute ago. Very pale. Very apologetic.
casualties.stays: Her legs won't hold her. She apologises for the fuss.
casualties.why: Over two seconds for the nail bed to pink up: she's losing blood somewhere. Red.

casualties.who: Old man with a sore hip
casualties.looks: Sitting on the kerb, asking somebody to find his spectacles.
casualties.stays: His hip won't let him stand. He'd like his spectacles.

casualties.looks: Blood down his face, shouting for his son, Ishaan.
casualties.walks: He's already up, searching the crowd for his son.

casualties.looks: Sitting up, dazed, ears ringing, eyebrows gone. His stall went up all at once.
casualties.stays: He stands, sways, and sits down hard.

casualties.who: Man fallen from the lighting tower
casualties.looks: Lying very still under the lighting tower. Breathing slowly, and noisily.
casualties.stays: Nothing. He snores.
casualties.why: Slow, noisy breathing and no answer to a command: his brain is in trouble. Red.

casualties.who: Young woman with a cut leg
casualties.looks: A dupatta tied tight round her calf. Glass from the bangle stall. She tied it herself. She's very calm.
casualties.stays: She can't stand on that leg. She doesn't try twice.
casualties.why: Over two seconds for the nail bed to pink up: the bleeding has beaten her knot. Red.

casualties.short: the man with the selfie stick
casualties.looks: Filming everything, narrating. A small cut over one eye.
casualties.walks: He walks to the gate, still filming, still narrating.

outbreak_rota.place: The surgical floor, in the outbreak
outbreak_rota.title: Outbreak cover

brief.easy: The bug's taken Lata and two others. Six patients, three of us, and half of them have the bug. Every bed gets a name. The rules are on the card.
brief.hard: Eight patients, four of us, and Ananya's still a student. Keep the bug away from the ones who can't fight it. I'll check it when you sign.
brief.extreme: Ten patients, five of us, and the bug in every other bed. No card, no help. You know the rules, Chief.

warn.load: {staff} can't carry that much. Somebody's three a.m. checks get missed.
warn.iv: {staff} isn't signed off for IV drugs here. {who} needs a nurse who can run that drip.
warn.infection: Not with {staff}. The same hands on an infection and on someone who can't fight one? That's how we lose a patient.
warn.confused: {who} needs watching, and {staff} will have too many to watch.
warn.student: {staff} is a student. {who} is too much for her on her own.

explain.load: More than one nurse can carry, and the checks get missed.
explain.iv: Only a nurse signed off for IV can give drugs through a drip.
explain.infection: Hands that touch an infection carry it to the patient who can't fight it.
explain.confused: A confused patient needs a nurse with time to watch them, or they wander and fall.
explain.student: A student can't take the heaviest patients alone.

signed.all: Signed. Every bed has a name, and nobody's carrying too much.
signed.gap: There's a bed with no name next to it, Chief.
signed.some: Signed. Somebody's carrying too much tonight.

staff.role: Theatre nurse, borrowed: the list is cancelled
Theatre nurse, borrowed for the night

patients.about: The stomach bug. A drip running, and a door kept shut.
Eighty-two, the stomach bug, and her kidneys struggling. Drip and hourly urine.
The stomach bug, nearly over. Eating rice and complaining about it.
Bowel operation yesterday. Drip, drain, pain pump. Keep the bug away.
On chemotherapy, with a fever. No white cells to spare.
Hernia repair this morning. Waiting for his son to drive him home.
Seventy-nine. The bug has left her muddled. She sets off for the bus stop at night.
Broken ankle in plaster. Needs help to the toilet, and asks politely every time.
The stomach bug, and six months pregnant. Drip, and the midwife twice a day.
Gallbladder out yesterday. Walking the corridor in his slippers.
Clear of the bug now, but dry as paper. Drip until she can drink.
Coming round from a head injury. Asks the date every ten minutes.
A nurse from Ward 3 who caught the bug. Wants to go back to work. She can't.
The bug, and a weak heart that can't take much fluid. Drip, and checks every hour.
Kidney transplant last year. On drugs that stop her fighting anything.
Ninety-one, deaf, and convinced he's on a train to Delhi.

cb_arif_history.about: 19 · pain that moved to the lower right
cb_arif_history.opening: Ask quickly, doctor. I have a thermodynamics exam at nine. Well. I had one.

questions.ask: Where did the pain start, and where is it now?
questions.answer: Round my belly button, last night after dinner. By two in the morning it had moved down here, low on the right. Now it hurts to walk.
questions.fact: Pain started round the navel, moved to the lower right overnight
questions.why: Pain that starts in the middle and settles low on the right is the appendix's story.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything?
questions.answer: Penicillin. At school my lips swelled up like a duck's and my mother still tells everyone at weddings.
questions.why: The usual antibiotic in theatre is a penicillin. The board must say so, or it goes straight into his drip.

questions.ask: Have you had a fever, or been sick?
questions.answer: Sick twice in the hostel bathroom. My roommate says I'm hot. He took my temperature with his hand. And then with a thermometer: thirty-eight.
questions.why: Fever and vomiting with that pain: the appendix is inflamed now. Waiting risks it bursting.

questions.ask: When did you last eat?
questions.answer: Hostel dinner at eight. Dal, rice, and something they called paneer. I didn't finish it, which is a first.

questions.ask: Have you taken anything for the pain?
questions.answer: Two painkillers from the chemist by the gate. They did nothing. The chemist said they'd do nothing. He was right.
questions.fact: Two painkillers from the chemist, no help

questions.ask: Have your bowels been normal?
questions.answer: Normal until yesterday. Nothing since. Is that... medical?

questions.ask: What's the exam?
questions.answer: Thermodynamics. Second year. Entropy always increases. That's the whole subject. Also my life.

questions.ask: Who are the four boys in the corridor?
questions.answer: My roommates. They carried me down three floors. They want to know if they can have my appendix for the lab.

cb_mohan_history.about: 54 · groin lump, stuck since this morning
cb_mohan_history.opening: Fast, please, doctor. I've got forty cylinders on the tempo and the driver's eating my lunch.

questions.ask: When did the lump appear, and does it go back in?
questions.answer: Two years, maybe three. It always went back when I lay down. This morning I lifted a cylinder on the third floor and it came out and stayed out. Hard as a stone.
questions.fact: Groin lump for two years, stuck since this morning
questions.why: A hernia that won't go back can trap bowel and cut off its blood. That makes it urgent: today, not next week.

questions.ask: When did you last eat?
questions.answer: Poha at five. A big plate. My wife says a man can't carry cylinders on an empty stomach.
questions.fact: Ate a plate of poha at five this morning
questions.why: A full stomach can come up into the lungs under anaesthetic. Dr. Khan needs to know, so she can protect his airway.

questions.ask: Have you been sick, or stopped passing wind?
questions.answer: Sick once, in the tempo. The driver wasn't pleased. And no wind since. My wife will say that's a miracle.
questions.fact: Vomited once, no wind since this morning
questions.why: Vomiting and no wind with a stuck hernia: the bowel inside is blocked. It can't wait for a list.

questions.ask: Which side is it?
questions.answer: Right side. The cylinder side. I always carry on the right.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything?
questions.answer: Nothing. Only to my supervisor.

questions.ask: Do you take any medicines?
questions.answer: One tablet for blood pressure. Every morning, with the poha.
questions.fact: Blood pressure tablet, taken this morning

questions.ask: How many floors do you climb a day?
questions.answer: Eighty, ninety. The new buildings have lifts. The lifts have notices saying no gas cylinders. So, stairs.

questions.ask: Do you have children?
questions.answer: Two daughters. One is studying to be a nurse. I'll tell her I met the Chief. She won't believe it.

cb_savitri_history.about: 66 · deep cut across the left palm
cb_savitri_history.opening: Ask, ask. My stall is shut and the whole bus stand is drinking bad tea from the other woman.

questions.ask: How did it happen?
questions.answer: Washing glasses at the stall, five o'clock. One cracked in my hand. Thick glass, the old kind. It went in deep.
questions.fact: Cut by a breaking glass while washing up
questions.why: Broken glass leaves slivers behind. Somebody has to look for them before the wound is closed.

questions.ask: When did you last have a tetanus injection?
questions.answer: Tetanus? When my son was born. He's twenty now. So... twenty years? Is that bad?
questions.fact: Last tetanus jab twenty years ago
questions.why: A dirty wound and a jab twenty years old: she needs a booster. The board says 'up to date' unless somebody asks.

questions.ask: Can you feel your fingertips, and move all your fingers?
questions.answer: I can feel them. I can move them. It hurts when I bend this one, but I can.
questions.fact: Feeling and movement in all fingers
questions.why: Feeling and movement mean the nerves and tendons are probably whole. That decides whether it's a stitch or a surgeon.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything?
questions.answer: No. Nothing. I've been stung by everything at that bus stand.

questions.ask: Do you take any medicines?
questions.answer: Sugar tablets. One in the morning. My sugar is good. Mostly. Except for the tea.

questions.ask: Which hand do you use most?
questions.answer: The right. This is the left. God was kind. Not very kind. A little kind.
questions.fact: Right-handed; the cut is on the left

questions.ask: How long have you had the stall?
questions.answer: Thirty-one years. Same corner. Three bus companies have gone bankrupt. My stall hasn't.

questions.ask: How much is a cup of your tea?
questions.answer: Ten rupees. For doctors, twelve. You can afford it.

cb_usha_history.about: 61 · pain under the right ribs, fever since last night
cb_usha_history.opening: I was a headmistress for twenty-two years. I'll know if you're not listening.

questions.ask: Tell me about the pain. Where is it, and when does it come?
questions.answer: Under my right ribs. It comes after meals, the rich ones. For three months. Last night, after my niece's engagement dinner, it came and didn't go.
questions.fact: Pain under the right ribs after rich meals, three months; constant since last night
questions.why: Pain under the right ribs after fatty food is the gallbladder's story: stones.

questions.ask: Do you take anything that thins the blood?
questions.answer: Aspirin, every morning, since my heart scare four years ago. The cardiologist said never miss it. I took it at seven.
questions.fact: Takes aspirin daily for her heart, took it at seven this morning
questions.why: Aspirin makes the liver bed ooze. The team needs to know, and keep blood ready.

questions.ask: Have you had a fever, or turned yellow?
questions.answer: A fever since midnight. My husband checked: thirty-eight point four. He wrote it down. He writes everything down.
questions.why: Fever means the gallbladder is inflamed now, not just full of stones. It needs to come out, not wait for a list.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything?
questions.answer: Nothing. Except bad grammar.

questions.ask: When did you last eat?
questions.answer: The engagement dinner, at ten last night. Biryani. Two helpings. I regret the second.

questions.ask: Have you been sick?
questions.answer: Once, at two in the morning. Into the bucket my husband had placed by the bed. He'd planned ahead.

questions.ask: Which school were you headmistress of?
questions.answer: The municipal girls' school by the station. Three of your nurses were my pupils. They still call me 'Ma'am'.

questions.ask: Was it a good engagement?
questions.answer: Very good. The boy is an engineer. They're always engineers.

cb_rosy_history.about: 83 · fell at home, can't stand on the left leg
cb_rosy_history.opening: I taught piano for fifty years, young doctor. I can hear a wrong note. Ask your questions.

questions.ask: How did you fall?
questions.answer: Over my cat, at six this morning. She sleeps on the second step. She has done for nine years. Today I forgot.
questions.fact: Tripped over her cat at six this morning
questions.why: An old person's fall at home: a broken hip until proven otherwise. The X-ray decides the operation.

questions.ask: Do you take anything that thins the blood?
questions.answer: Warfarin, for my irregular heart. I took it last night as always. The ambulance man said that's important. Your nurse gave me something yellow at breakfast.
questions.fact: On warfarin, last dose last night; vitamin K given this morning
questions.why: Warfarin makes a hip bleed like a tap. The team must know, check her clotting, and reverse it before they cut.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything?
questions.answer: Penicillin. In 1971 I swelled up like a balloon at my own recital. I finished the Chopin. Then I went to hospital.
questions.why: The usual antibiotic in theatre is a penicillin. The board must say so.

questions.ask: Where does it hurt?
questions.answer: The left hip, and down to the knee. When they lifted me it was like a thunderstorm.
questions.fact: Pain in the left hip, down to the knee

questions.ask: Who lives with you?
questions.answer: The cat. My niece comes on Sundays. Today is Wednesday, so I lay on the floor until the milkman came.
questions.fact: Lives alone; lay on the floor for an hour

questions.ask: When did you last eat?
questions.answer: Toast and marmalade at eight last night. Nothing since. I wasn't in a position to make breakfast.
questions.fact: Last ate at eight last night

questions.ask: What's the cat called?
questions.answer: Clementine. She is not sorry. Cats are never sorry.

questions.ask: Do you still play?
questions.answer: Every day. Scales at seven, Bach at eight. My neighbours set their clocks by me.

cb_gurdeep_history.about: 45 · lorry rolled over, steering wheel to the belly
cb_gurdeep_history.opening: Ask fast, doctor. Something inside isn't right. I've driven twenty-five years. I know when the engine's wrong.

questions.ask: What happened?
questions.answer: The bend at the top of the ghat. The brakes went soft, the lorry went over. The wheel hit me here, under the left ribs. Hard.
questions.fact: Lorry rolled; steering wheel hit him under the left ribs
questions.why: A heavy blow under the left ribs can split the spleen, and a split spleen bleeds into the belly where nobody can see.

questions.ask: Where does it hurt, and does it go anywhere?
questions.answer: Under the left ribs. And my left shoulder, which is strange. The wheel never touched my shoulder.
questions.fact: Pain under the left ribs and in the left shoulder tip
questions.why: Pain in the shoulder tip with a belly injury is blood under the diaphragm. It means bleeding inside.

questions.ask: Do you feel dizzy or thirsty?
questions.answer: Dizzy when I sit up. And so thirsty. I asked your nurse for water and she said no. Very politely.
questions.why: Dizzy and thirsty after a blow: he's losing blood. That is why he can't drink: he may need theatre soon.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything?
questions.answer: Nothing. Only to the toll booths.

questions.ask: When did you last eat?
questions.answer: Dhaba, at eleven. Dal and four rotis. Then the ghat.

questions.ask: Do you take any medicines?
questions.answer: Nothing. Sometimes a tablet for my back. Not today.

questions.ask: What were you carrying?
questions.answer: Onions. Eighteen tonnes. They're all over the ghat road now. The village will eat well this week.

questions.ask: Where were you driving?
questions.answer: Nashik to Hyderabad. Twice a week, twenty-five years. I know every pothole by name.

cb_anwar_history.opening: Ask, ask. But slowly. Every time I cough it gets worse, and I cough a lot.

questions.ask: When did the lump appear, and does it go back in?
questions.answer: A year. It came with the cough. It went back if I pushed. At dawn I coughed, and it came out and wouldn't go back. It's tight, and angry.
questions.fact: Groin lump for a year, stuck since dawn
questions.why: A hernia that won't go back can trap bowel and cut off its blood. That makes it urgent: today, not next week.

questions.ask: When did you last eat?
questions.answer: A paratha at five, after prayers, with my tea. Only one. My daughter-in-law makes them very big.
questions.fact: Ate a paratha at five this morning
questions.why: A full stomach can come up into the lungs under anaesthetic. Dr. Khan needs to know, so she can protect his airway.

questions.ask: Tell me about the cough.
questions.answer: Forty years of beedis. I stopped last year. The cough didn't. It's worst in the morning. Like a tractor starting.
questions.fact: Smoker's cough for years; stopped smoking last year
questions.why: A hard cough pushes on a weak spot, and after a repair it can burst the stitches. The repair has to be strong.

questions.ask: Which side is it?
questions.answer: The left. My tailor's tape says the left side of my trousers has been tighter for a year.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything?
questions.answer: No. Nothing. Not even to my daughter-in-law's cooking.

questions.ask: Do you take any medicines?
questions.answer: Cough syrup. Brown. It doesn't work, but it tastes of something.

questions.ask: You were a tailor?
questions.answer: Forty-five years. I made the Mayor's wedding suit. He's on his third wife. Still the same suit.

questions.ask: Do you have grandchildren?
questions.answer: Five. They all want phones. I want them to want books. Nobody's winning.

cb_kavita_history.about: 44 · pain under the right ribs since the night shift
cb_kavita_history.opening: I'm a bus conductor, doctor. I've heard every excuse. Don't give me one. Ask.

questions.ask: Tell me about the pain. Where is it, and when does it come?
questions.answer: Under my right ribs, into my back. It comes after food, for a few months. Last night on the late bus it came and stayed.
questions.fact: Pain under the right ribs into the back, after food, for months; constant since last night
questions.why: Pain under the right ribs after food is the gallbladder's story: stones.

questions.ask: Have you taken any painkillers or blood thinners?
questions.answer: Two aspirin at six this morning. I thought it was acidity. They did nothing, so I took the bus here instead.
questions.fact: Took two aspirin at six this morning
questions.why: Aspirin makes the liver bed ooze. The team needs to know, and keep blood ready.

questions.ask: Have you had a fever, or turned yellow?
questions.answer: Shivering since four. Hot, then cold. Not yellow. My mirror would have said.
questions.fact: Fever and shivering since four this morning, not yellow
questions.why: Fever means the gallbladder is inflamed now, not just full of stones. It needs to come out, not wait for a list.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything?
questions.answer: Nothing. Except passengers without change.

questions.ask: When did you last eat?
questions.answer: Vada pav at the depot, at eleven last night. Two. I won't lie to you.

questions.ask: Have you been sick?
questions.answer: Once, out of the bus window, between stops. Nobody noticed. It's that kind of route.

questions.ask: Which route do you work?
questions.answer: The forty-two. Station to the industrial estate and back, nine times a night. I could do it asleep. I nearly have.

questions.ask: Is anyone with you?
questions.answer: My son. He's sixteen and he's been on his phone since we arrived. He's very worried. That's how he shows it.

drill_hernia.opening: Mr. Rathod. Sixty-one, a hernia, an operation in the morning, and an opinion about everything. Ask.

questions.ask: Any heart trouble, or anything done to your chest?
questions.answer: A stent, two years back. A little tube in the heart pipe. I take the blood-thinning tablet every morning for it. The cardiologist was very strict.
questions.fact: Heart stent, on a blood thinner
questions.why: A stent and a blood thinner. Stop the tablet without the heart doctor and the stent can block; operate on it and he bleeds. Either way the surgeon has to know today.

questions.ask: Do you have diabetes, and what do you take for it?
questions.answer: Sugar, yes. Insulin, morning and night. My wife does the injection. I can't look.
questions.why: Insulin and no breakfast is a low sugar on the table. The dose and the timing have to be planned around the operation.

questions.ask: Has anyone in your family had trouble with an anaesthetic?
questions.answer: My brother. His temperature shot up during an operation and he nearly died. Hereditary something. They told him to tell all of us.
questions.fact: Brother had a severe reaction to anaesthetic
questions.why: A relative whose temperature shot up under anaesthetic can mean a rare inherited reaction. The anaesthetist needs different drugs and a plan, before, not during.

questions.ask: When did you last eat or drink?
questions.answer: Nothing since dinner. Tea at six this morning, with sugar. Is tea food?
questions.why: Sweet tea counts. Anything in the stomach can come back up under anaesthetic, so the time of the operation depends on his last drink.

questions.ask: Do you smoke, or have a cough?
questions.answer: Twenty a day for forty years. I cough in the mornings. Everyone does.
questions.fact: Smokes twenty a day, morning cough

questions.ask: Does the lump go back in when you lie down?
questions.answer: It goes back. It takes a while now, and it aches.

questions.ask: Have you had any operations before?
questions.answer: The stent, if that counts. And my appendix in college.

questions.ask: How's business at the shop?
questions.answer: Slow. People buy online now. Ask my son, he's the one who set it up. That's a question gone, Doctor.

questions.ask: Hot this week, isn't it?
questions.answer: I came about my hernia, not the forecast.

drill_gallstones.opening: Mrs. Joshi. Thirty-six, gallstones, a keyhole operation next week, and three children who all came along. Ask.

questions.ask: When was your last period, and could you be pregnant?
questions.answer: Six weeks ago. I'm usually like a clock. I thought it was the stress.
questions.fact: Period two weeks late, could be pregnant
questions.why: A late period before an operation means a pregnancy test first. The anaesthetic, the X-rays and the gas in the belly all change for a pregnancy.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything, even rubber gloves or plasters?
questions.answer: Rubber gloves. The kitchen ones bring me out in welts. And a plaster once took the skin off.
questions.why: A latex allergy on the table can be a full collapse. The whole theatre has to be set up latex-free before she comes in.

questions.ask: Any trouble with your breathing or your chest?
questions.answer: Asthma since school. Two puffs of the blue inhaler most days. More when it's dusty.
questions.fact: Asthma, uses the reliever most days
questions.why: Asthma that needs the reliever every day isn't controlled. Under anaesthetic that can turn into a tight chest. It needs sorting before, not during.

questions.ask: Do you take any medicines or tablets?
questions.answer: Just the inhaler. And iron tablets. The chemist said I looked pale.
questions.why: Pale and on iron tablets means somebody thinks she's anaemic. A blood count before surgery says whether she can afford to bleed.

questions.ask: When does the pain come, and what sets it off?
questions.answer: After anything fried. Under the ribs on the right, and round to my back. An hour of it and I can't sit still.
questions.fact: Pain after fried food, under the right ribs

questions.ask: Any fever, or have you ever turned yellow?
questions.answer: No fever. My sister says my eyes went yellow once. I didn't look.
questions.fact: Eyes may have gone yellow once

questions.ask: Have you had any operations before?
questions.answer: Three caesareans. The last one took a long time. They said there was scar tissue.

questions.ask: Are the children behaving?
questions.answer: The little one is eating the leaflets. That's one question, Doctor.

questions.ask: What do you cook at home?
questions.answer: Everything fried, which is probably why I'm here. Next question.

drill_hip.opening: Mr. Karim. Seventy-four, fell in his bathroom this morning, a broken hip, theatre as soon as it's safe. He's sharp, so don't talk down to him. Ask.

questions.ask: What happened just before you fell? Did you feel dizzy, or black out?
questions.answer: I stood up from the chair and the room went grey. The next thing, I was on the floor. I didn't trip. I know what tripping feels like.
questions.fact: Went grey and fell, didn't trip
questions.why: A fall after the room goes grey is a blackout, not a trip. The heart or the blood pressure dropped him, and it can do it again on the table unless it's found first.

questions.ask: Do you take any blood thinners?
questions.answer: Warfarin. For the heartbeat, it flutters. They check my blood every month.
questions.fact: On warfarin for a fluttering heart
questions.why: Warfarin means his blood doesn't clot. A hip operation on warfarin bleeds badly, so it has to be reversed first. The flutter explains the blackout too.

questions.ask: Did you hit your head? Can you remember everything?
questions.answer: There's a bump at the back. I don't remember the floor. I remember my daughter shouting.
questions.fact: Bump on the head, a gap in memory
questions.why: A bump and a gap in memory on a blood thinner can be a bleed inside the skull. That needs a scan before anything else.

questions.ask: When did you last eat or drink?
questions.answer: Breakfast at seven. Paratha. My daughter's. Then the floor.
questions.why: A full stomach fixes the earliest safe time for theatre. Emergency or not, the anaesthetist needs the hour.

questions.ask: Who's at home with you, and how do you get about?
questions.answer: My daughter, since my wife passed. I walk with a stick. I manage.
questions.fact: Lives with his daughter, walks with a stick

questions.ask: How is your eyesight?
questions.answer: A cataract in the left. The right one does the work. The bathroom light has gone, I keep saying.

questions.ask: Any pain in your chest, before or since?
questions.answer: No pain. A flutter, like I said. Like a bird in there.

questions.ask: Did your pension come through this month?
questions.answer: My hip is broken, Doctor. The pension can wait, and so can that question.

questions.ask: Did you see the match last night?
questions.answer: I'm seventy-four and lying on a trolley. Ask me something useful.

drill_stone.about: 45 · kidney stone, dye and X-ray tomorrow
drill_stone.opening: Mr. Sahu. Forty-five, a kidney stone, booked for tomorrow with the dye and the X-ray. He's in a hurry. Ask.

questions.ask: Has anything ever been wrong with your kidneys before?
questions.answer: I've only got one. They took the other out when I was a boy. Something was wrong with it. I forget to mention it.
questions.why: One kidney with a stone in it is a kidney that can shut down. The dye, the drugs and the timing all change when there is no spare.

questions.ask: Are you allergic to anything, including X-ray dye?
questions.answer: The dye. Last time they put it in I itched all over and my face swelled up. They gave me an injection.
questions.why: He reacted to the dye before, and the next time can be worse. The team needs to know before the dye is anywhere near him.

questions.ask: Any fever or shivering?
questions.answer: Shivering last night. Teeth chattering, then boiling hot. I thought it was the air conditioning.
questions.why: Fever with a blocked kidney is an infection behind the block. That's an emergency: the kidney has to be drained, not just the stone chipped.

questions.ask: When did you last eat or drink?
questions.answer: Lunch at one. Biryani. And a cold drink in the car.
questions.why: Lunch at one sets the earliest safe time for an anaesthetic. The stone can wait an hour or two. A full stomach can't be rushed.

questions.ask: How much do you drink in a day?
questions.answer: Coffee, mostly. Water when I remember. I'm in the car all day.

questions.ask: Have you had stones before?
questions.answer: Twice. They passed on their own, with a lot of shouting.

questions.ask: Any blood in your urine, or trouble passing it?
questions.answer: Pink, yesterday. And it burns.

questions.ask: Do you get to the gym?
questions.answer: I sell cars, Doctor. The gym is a thing other people do. Next.

questions.ask: Any holiday plans?
questions.answer: Goa, if you let me out. That's one question wasted, isn't it.
